The following metrics were compiled by the internal audit cell on 2025-08-31, covering all shelter master data records entered or modified between 2025-06-01 and 2025-08-31. The audit reviewed a stratified random sample of 1,200 records across all shelter IDs (SH-001 to SH-024), including capacity, occupancy, contact details, status codes, and remark fields. Error rates are expressed as a proportion of sampled records containing at least one substantive data entry error (e.g., incorrect capacity figure, transposed contact number, wrong status code, or misspelled shelter name). Minor formatting inconsistencies (e.g., date format variations, spacing) were noted but not counted as errors for this metric.

Audit methodology note: Two independent data entry operators re-entered the sampled records from source documents (shelter registration forms, site visit reports, and telephonic confirmations) and compared their outputs against the live database. Discrepancies were resolved by a senior auditor. Where a discrepancy could not be resolved due to missing source documentation, the record was excluded from the denominator and flagged for follow-up. A total of 14 records were excluded for this reason.

Remarks: Occupancy figure errors were the most common, often arising when daily headcount updates were entered late or from handwritten count sheets with unclear numerals. Contact number digit errors were typically transposition errors (e.g., 98900 vs 99800). Status code errors were frequently traced to shelters transitioning between ACTIVE and TEMPORARY statuses without timely database updates. Capacity figure errors were rare but serious, as they directly affect resource allocation decisions. Shelter name misspellings were minor but were corrected to standard names as per the DDMA shelter naming convention.

Minor formatting inconsistencies (e.g., date format variations, spacing) were noted but not counted as errors for this metric.

Audit methodology note: Two independent data entry operators re-entered the sampled records from source documents (shelter registration forms, site visit reports, and telephonic confirmations) and compared their outputs against the live database. Discrepancies were resolved by a senior auditor. Where a discrepancy could not be resolved due to missing source documentation, the record was excluded from the denominator and flagged for follow-up. Sahyog NGO Activity Reports – Volunteer Coordination (July–August 2025)
Prepared by: Field Coordination Desk, Sahyog Foundation, Pune
Period covered: 01 July 2025 – 31 August 2025
Audience: Sahyog management team, DDMA liaison officer
Distribution: Internal; copy to district administration cell

---

1. Overview

This report summarises volunteer registration, field deployment, and training activities coordinated by Sahyog NGO during the two-month period of July and August 2025. The period saw the onset of the southwest monsoon and subsequent localised flooding in low-lying wards, which required rapid mobilisation of volunteers for evacuation support, relief distribution, and shelter management. Coordination was carried out in close consultation with the district disaster management authority (DDMA) and the municipal corporation.

Key highlights for the period:

- The Sahyog NGO report states registered_volunteers 45 volunteers. Record status: current.
- Total field hours logged across all activities: 2,140 hours.
- New volunteers onboarded through the July orientation drive: 12.
- Training sessions conducted: 4 (two basic first-aid, one shelter management, one psychosocial first aid).
- Average attendance across training sessions: 38 participants.

The volunteer base remained largely stable through the reporting period, with the 45 registered volunteers forming the core pool for all deployments. Of these, 31 were actively deployed at least once during the two months; the remaining 14 were on standby or unavailable due to personal commitments, exams, or travel. We continue to maintain a waitlist of 9 prospective volunteers who have completed the preliminary application but have not yet completed the mandatory orientation.

---

2. Volunteer Registration Status (as of 31 August 2025)

The master volunteer register is maintained at the Sahyog office in digital format (Excel) with a physical backup. The register is updated within 48 hours of any change. The current status of the register is as follows:

| Deployed at least once | 31 | Field hours logged in section 3. |

Note: The register was reconciled on 15 August 2025. Three volunteers who had not responded to calls or messages since May 2025 were contacted and confirmed their continued interest. No removals were made during the period.

---

3. Field Activity Logs – July 2025

The month of July saw moderate rainfall and one significant flooding event in the low-lying areas near the Mula-Mutha riverbank. Sahyog volunteers were deployed for pre-monsoon awareness door-to-door visits, a mock drill conducted by the DDMA, and two days of relief distribution after localised waterlogging.

3.1 Pre-Monsoon Awareness Drive (1–5 July 2025)

Volunteers conducted door-to-door visits in the Warje and Karve Nagar areas, distributing pamphlets on emergency contact numbers, sandbag placement, and evacuation routes. A total of 620 households were covered.

3.2 Mock Drill with DDMA (18 July 2025)

Sahyog participated in the district-level mock drill organised by the DDMA at the Hadapsar flood zone. Six volunteers were deployed as observers and two as first-aid support. The drill simulated a flash flood scenario with a 30-minute evacuation window.

3.3 Relief Distribution – Waterlogging Response (24–25 July 2025)

Following heavy rain on the night of 23 July, waterlogging was reported in the Karve Nagar low-lying pockets. Sahyog coordinated with the ward office and distributed dry ration kits and water purification tablets.

---

August saw comparatively stable weather, with intermittent rain. Sahyog shifted focus to preparedness reviews, volunteer training, and a repeat door-to-door campaign in areas not fully covered in July.

A follow-up visit was conducted in the Warje and Kothrud areas to verify pamphlet retention and awareness of evacuation routes. The team also collected feedback on the July distribution.

- Households visited: 410
- Volunteers involved: 14

- Feedback summary: 82% of households recalled the emergency contact numbers; 11% requested a second copy of the route map.

Orientation for the newly onboarded volunteers (from the July drive) was held at the Sahyog office. The session covered the code of conduct, field safety, and basic first aid.

A half-day training session on radio communication protocols was conducted for 20 volunteers, including all coordinators. The session was a direct follow-up to the mock drill observation noted in Section 3.2.

- The pending orientation for the waitlist volunteers (9 applicants) is tentatively scheduled for the first week of September, subject to trainer availability.

**4. Summary of Volunteer Engagement (July–August)**

The July–August training cycle saw strong participation across all four core modules, with a total of 41 unique volunteers attending at least one session. Of these, 30 volunteers completed all four modules and are now eligible for the field deployment badge (yellow badge). The badge distribution is scheduled for the first Monday coordination call of September (08 Sep 2025).

The Community Engagement & Door-to-Door Survey Methods session on 09 August recorded the highest attendance of the cycle, with 34 volunteers present. The First Aid Refresher & Heat-Stress Management session on 30 August had the lowest attendance, with 28 volunteers, partly due to the holiday weekend and a last-minute venue change. The Radio Communication Protocols session on 23 August had 31 attendees, and the Volunteer Code of Conduct & Data Privacy session on 02 August had 29 attendees.

Volunteer hours logged for the two-month period totalled 1,245 hours, which includes training time, preparation work, and the two community outreach drives conducted in August (Hadapsar ward survey on 17 Aug and the monsoon preparedness door-to-door drive on 24 Aug). The average volunteer contributed approximately 30 hours over the period.

---

**5. Volunteer Feedback and Quotes**

After the final training session on 30 August, we asked volunteers to share their thoughts on the training cycle. A few of the responses are reproduced below (names withheld for privacy).

- "The radio communication session was the most useful for me. I had no idea how much coordination goes into a single field deployment. Now I feel confident about calling in a situation report." – Volunteer, Hadapsar team
- "The first aid refresher was practical and well-paced. The heat-stress management part is especially relevant for the coming months. I only wish we had more time for the hands-on practice." – Volunteer, Kondhwa team
- "The door-to-door survey methods session changed how I approach residents. The role-play exercises helped me understand how to ask sensitive questions without making people uncomfortable." – Volunteer, Wanowrie team
- "I appreciated that the Code of Conduct session was not just a list of do's and don'ts. The case studies made it real. I think every volunteer who goes into the field should attend this before any deployment." – Volunteer, Yerawada team

Volunteers also submitted 12 written feedback forms. The most common suggestions were:
1. Provide printed handouts for the radio communication protocols (5 requests).
2. Schedule future training sessions on weekdays rather than weekends, as some volunteers have family commitments on Sundays (4 requests).
3. Include a short demonstration of the first aid kit contents and their uses (3 requests).

These suggestions will be reviewed during the September coordination calls, and the training team will incorporate feasible changes into the next cycle (planned for November–December 2025).

---

**6. Challenges and Issues**

The following challenges were encountered during the July–August period. They are recorded here for reference and for the district (DDMA) liaison file.

**6.1 Venue availability for the 30 Aug session.** The originally confirmed venue (Hadapsar community hall) was double-booked by the ward office. We were informed on 27 August and had to shift the First Aid Refresher to the Sahyog office premises. The space was adequate for the 28 attendees, but the shift caused a 45-minute delay in the start time. Two volunteers who had confirmed attendance could not be reached in time and missed the session. This is one of the reasons the 30 Aug session had the lowest attendance.
